slides.title: Before you buy the brand, test the [goodwill].
slides.lede: A polished identity can conceal weak customer preference. An unremarkable one can sit behind a trusted name with real commercial value. The deal should tell them apart.

slides.title: Diligence asks what you are [actually buying]
slides.text: A design review may recommend a clearer identity. Diligence asks whether the brand supports demand, pricing power and retention, and whether the buyer can legally control it after closing.

items.title: Is demand genuinely brand-led?
items.text: Separate brand equity from general market demand.

items.title: Can the buyer control it?
items.text: Trademarks, licences, domains, contracts, creator rights.

items.title: Is the promise credible?
items.text: Delivery, reviews and complaints against positioning.

items.title: Can value survive integration?
items.text: Naming, architecture, governance and migration plans.

slides.title: Value that rests on something [the target does not control]
slides.note: Ask what happens if the relationship ends, changes ownership or demands higher fees. **That risk belongs in the commercial assumptions.**

slides.title: A registration is [not a complete answer]

cards.label: Lower risk
cards.text: Target owns registered marks in relevant classes and territories.

cards.label: Higher risk
cards.text: Mark owned by a founder, parent or affiliate, or held under licence.

slides.title: Renaming too quickly can [discard the recognition] you paid for
slides.text: Keeping every legacy name can confuse customers and duplicate marketing costs. Settle architecture, governance, customer migration and measurement before final naming decisions are announced.

slides.title: Know what you are buying before you sign.
slides.lede: Brand due diligence before an acquisition. Read the full guide via the link in our bio.
